chapter: Dancing schools and Charlie Johnson in New York
title: June Clark, trumpeter who lost his upper register
summary: McRae calls Clark one of the outstanding 1930s trumpeters, once rated with Armstrong, until a split lip left him unable to play high.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Tell us some more about June Clark. Not much seems to be known about him.
Well June Clark was one of the outstanding trumpet players back in the 30's.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
He also played at the Cotton Club. I think June Clark was at the Cotton Club before Duke and them went in there.
I understand he -- I think he played with Charlie Johnson there for a while too. And then he split his lip.

Evidently, he didn't wait till it healed up or it didn't heal up right or something. One of the nerves -- he was unable -- he could play, he could really play, but he was unable to hit any more high notes or go high like he used to go.
It used to strain if he make a high note. Something in that top nerve in that lip that didn't heal up right -- that muscle.
He couldn't hit any high -- he could blow, but he couldn't, you know -- he want to go upper register high, you know, he started going up the (inaudible) he couldn't make it.
He'd stay right in the middle of the horn. But hit a note now and then, you know. But he was a sensational trumpet player. He was considered one of the finest around in those days.

Somebody considered him as the great AS Louie at one time before he lost his lip -- you know, the pressure in his lip.
